title: Informed consent and material risk (Montgomery)
blurb: Seek valid consent from women for themselves and their newborns, disclosing material risks and reasonable alternatives as Montgomery requires.
question: A woman with insulin-treated diabetes is expecting a large baby. She has not been told about the risk of shoulder dystocia because 'she would only ask for a caesarean'. Which legal principle has been breached?

teach.body: Valid consent is given voluntarily, by a person with capacity, who has been properly informed. SPM 1.20 asks midwives to seek informed consent from women both for herself and for her newborn infant, and Code 4.2 requires properly informed consent, documented, before any action. In plain English: she freely says yes (or no) to something she understands, and she can change her mind at any time, even part way through.
teach.cite: SPM 1.20; NMC Code 4.2; DH Reference guide to consent (2009)

teach.caption: A signature is evidence of consent, not consent itself. Going along with care (acquiescence) is not consent.

teach.body: In 1999 Nadine Montgomery, who had insulin-dependent diabetes and was just over five feet tall, was expecting her first baby. She was not told of the 9 to 10% risk of shoulder dystocia, because her obstetrician felt most women told would ask for a caesarean. Shoulder dystocia occurred; the cord was occluded for about 12 minutes and her son was born with cerebral palsy and Erb's palsy. The Supreme Court found she would have chosen a caesarean if properly informed.
teach.cite: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 paras 7, 13, 22

rows.label: Consent form
values: Dialogue needed; form is not enough

children.edge: This woman, as you know or should know
children.label: Material: disclose
Not required, but she may ask

teach.caption: Materiality 'cannot be reduced to percentages': consider the nature of the risk, its effect on her life, the benefits she seeks and the alternatives (para 89).

items: Disclose material risks of recommended treatment AND reasonable alternative or variant treatments (para 87).
Use dialogue: make information comprehensible; do not bombard her or rely on a signature (para 90).
She may choose not to hear about risks; respect that and record it (para 85).
Therapeutic exception: withhold only if disclosure would be seriously detrimental to her health; it must not be used to steer her choice (paras 88, 91).
Necessity: urgent treatment of a woman who is unconscious or unable to decide (para 88).

Consent point

Parents may decline all or part; record, tell GP and HV
Verbal consent; SCD, CF, CHT declinable singly; IMDs as a group
teach.caption: SPM 1.20: consent from the woman for her newborn infant, as a person with parental responsibility.

teach.h: Scenario: Priya and a membrane sweep
teach.body: Priya is 40+2 weeks and her midwife, Hollie, offers a membrane sweep. Hollie explains what it involves, its purpose and possible side effects, and the reasonable alternatives: waiting, or discussing induction from 41+0. She asks what matters most to Priya and checks understanding. Priya agrees, and Hollie records the discussion and verbal consent. Midway, Priya says stop; Hollie stops at once, because consent can be withdrawn at any stage.

teach.text: The Montgomery test is NOT 'what would a responsible body of professionals disclose?' (that was Bolam/Sidaway). It is what a reasonable person in her position, or this particular woman, would attach significance to. And it covers reasonable alternatives, not just risks.

items: Valid consent: voluntary, informed, with capacity; can be withdrawn at any time, including during a procedure.
Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11 para 87: disclose material risks and reasonable alternatives.
Material = a reasonable person in her position, or this woman, would attach significance to it; not a percentage.
Dialogue, not a consent form; the therapeutic exception is narrow and must not steer her choice.
SPM 1.20: consent for herself and her newborn (vitamin K, NIPE, blood spot, hearing).

summary: You can now explain the elements of valid consent and apply the Montgomery material risk test in maternity care, including reasonable alternatives. You can also seek consent from parents for newborn care and screening.

A.q: Under Montgomery, which risks must a midwife or doctor disclose before recommended treatment?
options: Risks a responsible body of professionals would disclose
Risks above a 1% chance of occurring
Risks a reasonable person in her position would find significant
Risks listed on the trust's consent form
A.why: Para 87: a risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it, or the clinician knows or should know this patient would.

whyNot.0: This is the Bolam/Sidaway approach that Montgomery replaced.
whyNot.1: Para 89: materiality cannot be reduced to percentages.
whyNot.3: A form does not define what is material to her.

A.q: During a vaginal examination in labour, a woman says 'stop'. What should the midwife do?
options: Stop the examination
Finish quickly to avoid repeating it
Explain why it must be completed
Pause, then continue when she is calmer
A.why: Consent can be withdrawn at any time, including during a procedure; NG235 1.8.9 tells women they can ask to stop at any stage.

whyNot.1: Continuing after withdrawal of consent is examining without consent.
whyNot.2: She has withdrawn consent; persuasion is not appropriate at this moment.
whyNot.3: Continuing requires her fresh consent, not just calm.

A.q: What did the Supreme Court say about consent forms in Montgomery?
options: A signed form is conclusive proof that she was informed
Forms must be signed before every maternity intervention
Forms remove the need for a verbal explanation of risks
Routinely demanding a signature does not fulfil the duty
A.why: Para 90: the duty is not fulfilled by bombarding the patient with technical information, let alone by routinely demanding her signature on a consent form.

whyNot.0: A signature is evidence only; it does not prove she was informed.
whyNot.1: Much maternity care proceeds on verbal consent.
whyNot.2: Dialogue is the heart of the duty.

B.q: A midwife offers induction at 41+3 weeks. Which information is required by Montgomery as well as the risks of induction?
options: Reasonable alternatives, such as monitoring
The unit's induction waiting times
The obstetrician's personal preference
Her chance of a vaginal birth next time
B.why: Para 87: disclose material risks AND reasonable alternative or variant treatments. Expectant management with additional monitoring is a reasonable alternative (NG207).

whyNot.1: Waiting times may be useful, but Montgomery requires alternatives to be discussed.
whyNot.2: Personal preference is not material information.
whyNot.3: Future birth outcomes may matter to some women, but the requirement here is reasonable alternatives.

B.q: Parents decline the newborn blood spot test for cystic fibrosis but accept the others. What should the midwife do?
options: Explain that all conditions must be tested
Defer the whole test until they agree
Ask the paediatrician to obtain consent
Test for all conditions except cystic fibrosis
B.why: Parents can decline screening for sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis and congenital hypothyroidism individually (the inherited metabolic diseases only as a group). Their choice is recorded.

whyNot.1: Deferring delays screening for conditions they have accepted.
whyNot.2: Midwives can take this consent; no referral is needed.

B.q: A woman says she does not want to hear about the risks of an epidural; she just wants one. What does Montgomery say?
options: Risks must be explained before it is sited
The anaesthetist must decide what to tell her
She can choose not to discuss risks
Her partner should be told the risks instead
B.why: Para 85: a person can decide she does not wish to be informed of risks, and the clinician is not obliged to discuss them. This should be recorded, and she can ask later.

whyNot.0: Montgomery accepts that she may choose not to be told.
whyNot.1: Montgomery moved the focus from the professional's view to the patient's.
whyNot.3: Her information is confidential; telling her partner is not a substitute.

C.q: A consultant decides not to mention the small risk of uterine rupture during VBAC, saying, 'If I tell her, she'll choose a repeat caesarean, which is worse for her'. Is this a valid use of the therapeutic exception?
options: Yes, because the consultant thinks it best
Yes, because the risk is less than 1%
No, because exceptions apply to babies
No, it is being used to steer her choice
C.why: Para 91: the therapeutic exception must not be used to prevent a patient making an informed choice the doctor considers contrary to her best interests. It applies only where disclosure would be seriously detrimental to her health.

whyNot.0: Professional preference is exactly what para 91 forbids as a reason.
whyNot.1: Materiality cannot be reduced to percentages; a rare but serious risk may be material.
whyNot.2: The exception concerns the patient's own health, not babies.

C.q: A woman with type 1 diabetes and an estimated fetal weight above the 97th centile asks about birth options. Which approach best reflects Montgomery?
options: Recommend vaginal birth and mention caesarean if asked
Discuss shoulder dystocia risk and the option of caesarean
Book a caesarean without discussing other options
Explain that the obstetrician will choose the safest mode
C.why: Montgomery itself concerned this situation: a diabetic woman with a large baby must be told of the shoulder dystocia risk and the reasonable alternative of caesarean, so she can make an informed choice.

whyNot.0: Waiting for her to ask is what went wrong in Montgomery.
whyNot.2: Booking without discussion removes her choice.
whyNot.3: The decision is hers, made with information from the team.

C.q: A woman who agreed to a fetal blood sample in established labour becomes very distressed and says 'I can't do this'. The registrar says, 'You consented earlier'. What should the midwife do?
options: Advocate for her and stop to clarify her wishes
Support the registrar, as consent was given
Ask her partner to confirm the earlier consent
Hold her legs so the sample can be taken quickly
C.why: Consent can be withdrawn at any time, including during a procedure (DH guide para 45). The midwife advocates for the woman (SPM 1.15, Code 3.4) and the procedure stops while her wishes are clarified.

whyNot.1: Earlier consent does not override withdrawal.
whyNot.2: Her partner cannot confirm consent on her behalf.
whyNot.3: Restraining her would be an assault without valid consent.

reteach.title: Consent as a conversation
reteach.question: If consent were a conversation rather than a form, what would you need to cover?

blocks.body: What is being offered and why. The material risks: what would matter to her. The reasonable alternatives, including doing nothing or waiting. What she values and wants. Then check understanding, let her decide, and tell her she can change her mind. Record the conversation, not just the outcome.

blocks.text: 'She signed the form' does not mean she was informed. 'She agreed earlier' does not stop her withdrawing now.

explain.body: Voluntary, informed, with capacity. Can be verbal or non-verbal. A signature is evidence only. Can be withdrawn at any time, including during a procedure.

test.q: A woman holds out her arm when the midwife says she needs to take blood. What does this represent?
options: Non-verbal consent
Acquiescence, not consent
Implied refusal
Invalid consent without a form
test.why: Consent can be non-verbal, such as holding out an arm, when she understands what is proposed.

whyNot.1: Acquiescence is going along without understanding; here she actively offers her arm.
whyNot.3: A form is not required for valid consent.

explain.body: Para 87: a reasonable person in her position, or this particular woman, would attach significance to the risk. Para 89: not reduced to percentages.

test.q: According to Montgomery, how is the materiality of a risk assessed?
options: By a fixed percentage threshold
By peer professional opinion
By its significance to her
By the trust's risk register
test.why: Material risks are those a reasonable person in her position, or she herself, would attach significance to.

whyNot.0: Para 89: materiality cannot be reduced to percentages.
whyNot.1: Peer opinion was the old Bolam approach.
whyNot.3: A risk register is an organisational tool, not the legal test.

explain.body: Therapeutic exception: disclosure would be seriously detrimental to health (narrow; not to steer choice). Necessity: urgent treatment when she is unconscious or unable to decide. She may also decline to hear risks.

rows.label: Misuse
values: Using it when she can decide

test.q: When does the necessity exception in Montgomery apply?
options: When she is distressed by hearing the information
When treatment is urgent and she cannot decide
When the team is short of time in labour
When the risk is under 1% for this woman
test.why: Para 88: the clinician is excused from conferring when treatment is urgent and the patient is unconscious or otherwise unable to make a decision.

whyNot.0: Distress does not remove her ability to decide.
whyNot.2: Workload is not a legal exception.

explain.body: SPM 1.20: seek consent from the woman for her newborn. Vitamin K, NIPE, blood spot and hearing screening are offered; parents may decline, and choices are recorded and shared with the GP and health visitor.

test.q: Parents decline part of the NIPE newborn examination. What should the midwife do?
options: Complete it, as it is a national screen
Ask the paediatrician to examine the baby
Record the decision and inform the GP and HV
Delay discharge until they agree
test.why: NIPE handbook: parents may decline all or part of the examination; the decision is recorded and the GP and health visitor informed.

whyNot.1: A paediatric examination would also need consent.
whyNot.3: Delaying discharge to obtain agreement is coercive.
